This, I think, is an important fact to keep in mind. While the
formal process of the meeting follows a set pattern, the substance
does not. There is no attempt prior to meetings to poll the FOMC
members together on a policy recommendation, and there would be
strenuous resistance if that were attempted. Even in the coffee break
prior to the policy discusslon. there is little, if any, consensus building.
Rather, the meeting itself is the place for honest, open discussion
about both our economic philosophies and how they should be
reflected in policy.
These past four years have been an extraordinarily interesting
time to be on the Committee from a substance perspective. In general,
setting monetary policy is easier when all the signs point in the same
direction. For example, the combination of tight markets, low
unemployment, and prospects for unsustainable rates of economic
growth, all suggest a tighter policy is necessary. Conversely, high
unemployment, prospects for slow or negative growth, and little price
pressure suggest a more accommodative policy. But things aren't so
easy when, as has happened over much of the past several years,

there is at times no compelling need for policy change, only upside or
downside risks to be understood and avoided.
By any rational measure of economic policy, we seem to have
achieved the economic equivalent of nirvana, at least domestically--low
unemployment, continued underlying sources of solid economic growth
in consumer and business spending; interest rates that while rising
don't seem at the present to have significantly affected housing
markets and business finance; very few price or wage pressures;
ebullient though at times volatile stock and bond markets; and a fiscal
deficit that has essentially disappeared. Even many of our recent
challenges on the international front are fading.
This has been the longest period of peacetime expansion in
recorded U.S. economic history, and by February stands a good chance
of becoming the longest expansion, in peacetime or otherwise. The
real issue is how to keep it on track, recognizing that our record of
smoothing out and extending growth cycles, while improving of late, is
anything but perfect. History teaches that most growth phases end
not because they wane on their own, but because resource constraints

bind too much, inflation accelerates and the Fed has to step on the
brakes. This growth phase has been in many ways, unique, but in my
view anyway, caution about the potential risks is warranted.
Have things really changed out there in the labor markets with
globalization, technology, and ever increasing competition so that wage
pressures are permanently lower at any given level of unemployment?
It is tempting to believe this is true, but do we have enough confidence
in the data so far to avoid the surge in inflation we experienced in late
'89 when similar arguments were made? Has all the investment in
computers and productive capacity changed our underlying ability to
grow to the extent that more workers can be absorbed than we could
expect from historical relationships? What effect do rising asset prices
have on consumer spending and business investment, and will these
trends reverse if asset prices fall or flatten out? And how does the
prospect of stronger foreign growth and a weaker dollar affect the
balance of inflation risks faced by monetary policy makers?

To reiterate some economic basics, over time, the long-run
growth rate of the. economy can for all practical purposes only be
increased through higher rates of productivity. In turn, higher rates of
productivity growth can only be achieved through higher rates of
domestic savings and investment. And, finally, higher rates of saving
and investment will occur most readily in an environment in which the
threat or reality of inflation does not distort the decisions of savers or
investors. I think we have only to look at the progress this country has
made since 1982, when the back of the high rates of 1970s inflation
was essentially broken, to recognize the benefits that can be realized
from a restrained inflationary environment in terms of increased
international competitiveness and a renewed emphasis on productive
investment.

deeply rooted in the public interest.
Now, let me turn to near-term prospects for the economy as I see
them. As I noted earlier, we are experiencing one of the longest
periods of sustained growth, low inflation, and low unemployment in
recorded U.S. economic history. Indeed, one has to go back to the
'60s to see periods of similar success.

the degree to which this success has been unexpected--in fact, most
forecasters have been wrong about growth (on the low side) and about
inflation (on the high side) for several years.
Over the past four quarters, the economy has grown at a pace of
3.9 percent, well ahead of what most forecasters expected. Reflecting

this, and the fact that about 2.5 million net new jobs were added
during the past year, the unemployment rate has fallen to 4.2 percent.
These signals of capacity constraint in the face of growth that
continues above the long-term trend could signal higher rates of
inflationary growth. But, as yet, we see almost no signs of increasing
price pressures. Core inflation has declined over one-half percentage
point to 1 .9 percent at an annual rate over the past year. Here again,
most forecasters were too pessimistic, expecting inflation to drift
upwards.
Looking forward, the real fundamentals continue to look positive,
but there are risks as well. Job growth and personal income are strong
and these are the primary drivers of consumption. Consumer
confidence remains in a high range and consumer spending on
automobiles and other big-ticket durables is advancing at double-digit
rates this year. In fact, over the course of this expansion, spending on
durables has grown about twice as fast as consumer income and GDP.
Residential investment continues to be strong, supported by
income growth, capital gains and good levels of affordability, despite

an increase in long-term interest rates of better than one percentage
point last year. Business investment has been strong and will likely
continue even in the face of the slowing profit growth seen in 1999
and expected for 2000. In fact, as Asia recovers, U.S. manufacturing,
especially that related to merchandise exports, is rebounding as well.
But for both consumers and businesses, rising levels of debt are a fact
of life. In particular the personal savings rate is negative, as consumers
continue to spend more than they earn, and the consumer debt burden
relative to income is trending upward. Clearly, there is less capacity to
withstand problems now than earlier in this cycle.
Aside from the risks presented by rising debt, other worrisome
trends are apparent. The first of these involves the burgeoning foreign
trade deficit driven by rapid growth of imports. After a huge decline in
1998, export growth is beginning to rebound, though the trade deficit
widened to historically high levels this summer. Foreign growth should
spur demand for U.S. exports, and a weaker dollar should dampen the
domestic appetite for foreign goods. However, both these trends do
not augur well for managing pressures on recources or cost growth.

Finally, while inflation growth has been quite low, resource
constraints, especially in labor markets, are significant and not
expected to wane. Increasing rates of productivity have formed the
wedge between labor market tightness and inflation, but how long this
can continue is a real question. Temporary factors restraining inflation
such as commodity price declines, slow external growth and low
benefit cost increases are now waning. Thus, inflation remains a key
risk and a worry for central bankers. On the international scene the
financial turmoil and trauma of the Russian and Asian crises seem far
behind us now, and the policy easing introduced last fall largely has
been reversed. The question now is whether this will be enough.
In sum, the U.S. economy is strong and likely will remain so for at
least the rest of this year and the first half of next year. The risks of
inflationary pressure are real, but with a great deal of care--and some
luck--my hope is we will be able to extend this period of balanced, low
inflationary growth.
